claim: Secondary-active transporters are found in all domains of life.
source: Secondary-active transporters are found in all domains of life (Ren and Paulsen, 2005; Pao et al., 1998; Reizer et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Secondary-active transporters catalyse the movement of molecules across membranes by exploiting the free energy associated with electrochemical ion gradients.
source: They catalyse the movement of molecules across membranes, exploiting the free energy associated with electrochemical ion gradients to drive transport (see Drew et al., 2021; Bosshart and Fotiadis, 2019 for recent reviews on the topic).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent review articles

claim: In bacteria, secondary-active transporters are used for both the export of toxic compounds and for the import of nutrients needed for cell growth.
source: In bacteria, secondary-active transporters are used for both the export of toxic compounds and for the import of nutrients needed for cell growth (Drew et al., 2021; Henriquez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The import of carbohydrates across the plasma membrane is a key process for bacteria, particularly pathogenic bacteria that adopt a scavenging lifestyle within their host.
source: The import of carbohydrates across the plasma membrane is a key process for bacteria, particularly those pathogenic bacteria that adopt a scavenging lifestyle within their host (Vimr, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: For Haemophilus influenzae, the ability to uptake host-derived sialic acids is important for pathogenesis.
source: For Haemophilus influenzae, a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen, the ability to uptake host-derived sialic acids is important for pathogenesis (Apicella, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Sialic acids are a diverse family of nine-carbon carbohydrates.
source: Sialic acids are a diverse family of nine-carbon carbohydrates, and in humans, sialic acids are highly abundant in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts where they coat glycoconjugates as terminal sugars (Vimr, 2013; Cohen and Varki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature and represents established biochemical knowledge

claim: In humans, sialic acids are highly abundant in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts where they coat glycoconjugates as terminal sugars.
source: Sialic acids are a diverse family of nine-carbon carbohydrates, and in humans, sialic acids are highly abundant in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts where they coat glycoconjugates as terminal sugars (Vimr, 2013; Cohen and Varki, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The most common sialic acid found in humans is N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac).
source: The most common sialic acid found in humans is N-acetylneuraminate (Neu5Ac) (Vimr, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Bacteria such as H. influenzae evolved the ability to utilise host-derived sialic acid as a nutrient source.
source: To gain a growth advantage in these environments, bacteria such as H. influenzae evolved the ability to utilise host-derived sialic acid as a nutrient source (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1 which illustrates the sialic acid utilization pathway

claim: The sialic acid catabolic pathway provides an alternative source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy.
source: The sialic acid catabolic pathway provides an alternative source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy, and has been identified in 452 bacterial species, most of which are mammalian pathogens or commensals (McDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The sialic acid catabolic pathway has been identified in 452 bacterial species, most of which are mammalian pathogens or commensals.
source: The sialic acid catabolic pathway provides an alternative source of carbon, nitrogen, and energy, and has been identified in 452 bacterial species, most of which are mammalian pathogens or commensals (McDonald et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature providing specific quantitative data

claim: H. influenzae uses sialic acids to coat its lipopolysaccharide surface, and this sialylation provides camouflage and protection from the human immune response.
source: Alongside degradation, and perhaps more importantly, H. influenzae uses sialic acids to coat its lipopolysaccharide surface, and this sialylation in turn provides camouflage and protection from the human immune response (Severi et al., 2005; Allen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: H. influenzae lacks the de novo sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, so sialic acids must be scavenged and transported into the cell.
source: H. influenzae lacks the de novo sialic acid biosynthetic pathway, so sialic acids must be scavenged and transported into the cell (Vimr et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Engineered H. influenzae strains that are unable to transport sialic acids into the cell have decreased virulence in animal models.
source: Engineered H. influenzae strains that are unable to transport sialic acids into the cell have decreased virulence in animal models—evidence that the sialic acid transport pathway is a viable therapeutic target (Jenkins et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature describing experimental results

claim: The sialic acid transport pathway is a viable therapeutic target.
source: Engineered H. influenzae strains that are unable to transport sialic acids into the cell have decreased virulence in animal models—evidence that the sialic acid transport pathway is a viable therapeutic target (Jenkins et al., 2010)
evidence: Inferred from experimental evidence showing decreased virulence when transport is blocked

claim: Inhibitors of sialic acid transporters have been developed.
source: and others have already developed inhibitors of sialic acid transporters (Bozzola et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The sole sialic acid transporter in H. influenzae belongs to the tripartite ATP-independent periplasmic (TRAP) transporter family.
source: The sole sialic acid transporter in H. influenzae belongs to the tripartite ATP-independent periplasmic (TRAP) transporter family.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about H. influenzae

claim: TRAP transporters are a major class of secondary-active transporters found only in bacteria and archaea.
source: TRAP transporters are a major class of secondary-active transporters found only in bacteria and archaea (Kelly and Thomas, 2001; Rosa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: TRAP transporters use energetically favourable cation gradients to drive the import of specific carboxylate-containing nutrients against their concentration-gradient.
source: They use energetically favourable cation gradients to drive the import of specific carboxylate-containing nutrients against their concentration-gradient, including C4-dicarboxylates, α-keto acids, aromatic substrates, amino acids, and sialic acids (Vetting et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: TRAP transporters import C4-dicarboxylates, α-keto acids, aromatic substrates, amino acids, and sialic acids.
source: They use energetically favourable cation gradients to drive the import of specific carboxylate-containing nutrients against their concentration-gradient, including C4-dicarboxylates, α-keto acids, aromatic substrates, amino acids, and sialic acids (Vetting et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A functional TRAP system is made up of a soluble substrate-binding 'P-subunit', and a membrane-bound complex comprising a small 'Q-subunit' and a large 'M-subunit'.
source: A functional TRAP system is made up of a soluble substrate-binding 'P-subunit', and a membrane-bound complex comprising a small 'Q-subunit' and a large 'M-subunit'.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TRAP transporter architecture

claim: For most TRAP transporters, the Q- and M-subunits are separate polypeptides.
source: For most TRAP transporters, the Q- and M-subunits are separate polypeptides (Mulligan et al., 2011; Mulligan et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: In ~25% of TRAP transporter sequences, the Q- and M-subunit polypeptides are fused into a single polypeptide.
source: but in ~25% of sequences (InterPro analysis; Blum et al., 2021) the Q- and M-subunit polypeptides are fused into a single polypeptide (Kelly and Thomas, 2001).
evidence: Supported by InterPro database analysis and citations

claim: TRAP transporters can only accept substrates from the P-subunit.
source: TRAP transporters are different from almost all other secondary-active transporters in that they can only accept substrates from the P-subunit (Scheepers et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The P-subunit is secreted into the periplasm to capture host-derived substrates with high affinity and specificity.
source: Analogous to ABC importers, the P-subunit is secreted into the periplasm to capture host-derived substrates with high affinity and specificity.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about TRAP transporter mechanism

claim: The substrate-loaded P-subunit delivers the substrate to the membrane transporter (Q- and M-subunits).
source: The substrate-loaded P-subunit subsequently delivers the substrate to the membrane transporter (Q- and M-subunits) (Vetting et al., 2015; Müller et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2008; Gangi Setty et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The SiaPQM system from H. influenzae has fused Q- and M-subunits.
source: The SiaPQM system from H. influenzae has fused Q- and M-subunits and is one of the best characterised TRAP systems to date (Severi et al., 2005; Müller et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The SiaPQM system from H. influenzae is one of the best characterised TRAP systems to date.
source: The SiaPQM system from H. influenzae has fused Q- and M-subunits and is one of the best characterised TRAP systems to date (Severi et al., 2005; Müller et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2008; Fischer et al., 2015; Peter et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature on this system

claim: The transport mechanism of SiaPQM is driven by a Na+ gradient.
source: with key functional and biophysical studies informing a putative transport mechanism driven by a Na+ gradient (Mulligan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: H. influenzae is sialidase negative and relies on the sialidases of other bacteria to generate free sialic acids.
source: H. influenzae is, however, sialidase negative and relies on the sialidases of other bacteria to generate free sialic acids (Lichtensteiger and Vimr, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: In Gram-negative bacteria, sialic acids diffuse into the periplasm through an outer membrane porin.
source: In Gram-negative bacteria, sialic acids diffuse into the periplasm through an outer membrane porin, such as the general porins OmpF or OmpC in many bacteria, Omp P2 in H. influenzae (Vachon et al., 1985; Munson et al., 1992), or by using a Neu5Ac specific porin such as NanC (Wirth et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: SiaP binds Neu5Ac in the periplasm with high-affinity, undergoing a ligand-induced conformational change to a closed state.
source: The substrate-binding protein SiaP (P-subunit) binds Neu5Ac in the periplasm with high-affinity, undergoing a ligand-induced conformational change to a closed state (Müller et al., 2006; Johnston et al., 2008; Gangi Setty et al., 2014; Fischer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The closed form of SiaP delivers Neu5Ac to the membrane bound Q- and M-subunits.
source: It is this closed form that then delivers Neu5Ac to the membrane bound Q- and M-subunits.
evidence: Inferred from the established mechanism of TRAP transporters

claim: The protein–protein interaction between SiaP and SiaQM and the subsequent transport of Neu5Ac through the transmembrane subunits are not yet characterised.
source: This protein–protein interaction and the subsequent transport of Neu5Ac through the transmembrane subunits are not yet characterised.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The binding of the closed P-subunit must induce either a global elevator-type motion or a local gating rearrangement as a part of an elevator mechanism.
source: In particular, the conformational changes that take place for both SiaP and SiaQM to allow alternating access of the transporter have not been fully elucidated, though we have suggested previously that the binding of the closed P-subunit must induce either a global elevator-type motion or a local gating rearrangement as a part of an elevator mechanism (Davies et al., 2023).
evidence: Based on previous work by the authors, representing a hypothesis

claim: The cryo-EM structure of HiSiaQM was determined at 2.99 Å resolution with local resolution extending to ~2.2 Å.
source: Here, we report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of HiSiaQM in amphipol and demonstrate that in detergent, amphipol, and a nanodisc environment, the fused H. influenzae SiaQM membrane subunits can stably exist as both monomeric (QM) and homodimeric (2QM) states. We determined the homodimeric (2QM) structure of HiSiaQM using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, the first structure of a fused TRAP transporter at near atomic resolution (2.99 Å, with local resolution extending to ~2.2 Å)
evidence: Experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination reported in this manuscript

claim: This is the first structure of a fused TRAP transporter at near atomic resolution.
source: We determined the homodimeric (2QM) structure of HiSiaQM using single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, the first structure of a fused TRAP transporter at near atomic resolution (2.99 Å, with local resolution extending to ~2.2 Å)
evidence: Comparison with existing literature showing this is a novel achievement

claim: HiSiaQM can stably exist as both monomeric (QM) and homodimeric (2QM) states in detergent, amphipol, and nanodisc environments.
source: Here, we report the high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structure of HiSiaQM in amphipol and demonstrate that in detergent, amphipol, and a nanodisc environment, the fused H. influenzae SiaQM membrane subunits can stably exist as both monomeric (QM) and homodimeric (2QM) states.
evidence: Experimental observations from multiple biochemical and biophysical experiments reported in this manuscript

claim: HiSiaQM operates using the 'elevator-with-an-operator' mechanism.
source: The structure, combined with functional and biophysical data, supports the hypothesis that HiSiaQM operates using the 'elevator-with-an-operator' mechanism that we proposed for TRAP transporters (Davies et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by structural, functional, and biophysical data presented in this manuscript and previous work

claim: Lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (L-MNG) led to more stable protein preparations compared to dodecyl-β-d-maltoside (DDM).
source: We assessed the stability of HiSiaQM in several detergents that solubilise HiSiaQM from Escherichia coli membranes. Lauryl maltose neopentyl glycol (L-MNG) led to more stable protein preparations compared to dodecyl-β-d-maltoside (DDM) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Experimental comparison of detergents shown in supplementary figure

claim: HiSiaQM purified with a high L-MNG concentration elutes as a major peak at 65 mL with a significant shoulder at 58 mL.
source: Curiously, HiSiaQM purified with a high L-MNG concentration elutes as a major peak at 65 mL with a significant shoulder at 58 mL, and this elution profile is reversed at a low L-MNG concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography shown in supplementary figure

claim: The elution profile of HiSiaQM is reversed at a low L-MNG concentration compared to high L-MNG concentration.
source: Curiously, HiSiaQM purified with a high L-MNG concentration elutes as a major peak at 65 mL with a significant shoulder at 58 mL, and this elution profile is reversed at a low L-MNG concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)—a signature of a self-association, suggesting HiSiaQM forms higher order oligomers.
evidence: Experimental data from size-exclusion chromatography shown in supplementary figure

claim: The elution profile of HiSiaQM is a signature of a self-association, suggesting HiSiaQM forms higher order oligomers.
source: and this elution profile is reversed at a low L-MNG concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a)—a signature of a self-association, suggesting HiSiaQM forms higher order oligomers.
evidence: Inference from the observed elution behavior in size-exclusion chromatography

claim: The non-fused monomeric Photobacterium profundum SiaQM (PpSiaQM) does not show self-association behavior when purified in low concentration of L-MNG.
source: By comparison, the non-fused monomeric Photobacterium profundum SiaQM (PpSiaQM) does not show this behaviour when expressed with the same purification tag and purified in the same low concentration of L-MNG, eluting at 67 mL, which we have previously shown to correspond to a monomeric species (Davies et al., 2023; Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Experimental comparison with PpSiaQM shown in supplementary figure and supported by previous publication

claim: Dimeric HiSiaQM exists either as a side-by-side parallel dimer where both monomers face the same way, or an antiparallel dimer where one monomer is rotated around the dimer interface 180° relative to the other.
source: HiSiaQM comprises two distinct dimeric configurations in approximately equal quantities (36%) in the 14,281-image dataset (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1). Dimeric HiSiaQM exists either as a side-by-side parallel dimer where both monomers face the same way, or an antiparallel dimer where one monomer is rotated around the dimer interface 180° relative to the other (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Structural data from cryo-EM analysis shown in figures

claim: The two dimeric configurations of HiSiaQM are present in approximately equal quantities (36% each) in the dataset.
source: HiSiaQM comprises two distinct dimeric configurations in approximately equal quantities (36%) in the 14,281-image dataset (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Quantitative data from cryo-EM particle classification

claim: Dimerisation is mediated by the same interface in both parallel and antiparallel structures.
source: Dimerisation is mediated by the same interface in both of these structures but given that HiSiaP is found in the periplasm and SiaQM requires SiaP to function, the parallel dimer is almost certainly the physiologically relevant conformation.
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM structures

claim: The parallel dimer is almost certainly the physiologically relevant conformation.
source: Dimerisation is mediated by the same interface in both of these structures but given that HiSiaP is found in the periplasm and SiaQM requires SiaP to function, the parallel dimer is almost certainly the physiologically relevant conformation.
evidence: Inference based on the known location of SiaP and functional requirements

claim: The overall resolution is 2.99 Å for the antiparallel dimer and 3.36 Å for the parallel dimer (FSC = 0.143 criterion).
source: The maps are of high resolution (overall 2.99 Å for the antiparallel dimer and 3.36 Å for the parallel dimer, FSC = 0.143 criterion) with both extending to 2.2 Å at the core, allowing for accurate fitting of helices and (almost) all side chains (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Quantitative data from cryo-EM structure determination

claim: Both maps extend to 2.2 Å at the core, allowing for accurate fitting of helices and (almost) all side chains.
source: The maps are of high resolution (overall 2.99 Å for the antiparallel dimer and 3.36 Å for the parallel dimer, FSC = 0.143 criterion) with both extending to 2.2 Å at the core, allowing for accurate fitting of helices and (almost) all side chains (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Structural data from cryo-EM maps shown in supplementary figure

claim: The dimeric particles allowed for structure determination without a protein fiducial marker bound.
source: The dimeric particles allowed for structure determination without a protein fiducial marker bound (e.g., nanobody or antigen-binding fragment), which was required to solve the structure of the monomeric PpSiaQM (Davies et al., 2023) and the lower resolution monomeric HiSiaQM (Peter et al., 2022).
evidence: Methodological observation comparing this work to previous studies

claim: In all four HiSiaQM protomers, the transport domain is in the inward-open conformation ('elevator down').
source: In all four HiSiaQM protomers, the transport domain is in the inward-open conformation ('elevator down'), which is the substrate release state (r.m.s.d. for alignment = ~0.2 Å, Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM structures shown in figures

claim: The inward-open conformation is the substrate release state.
source: In all four HiSiaQM protomers, the transport domain is in the inward-open conformation ('elevator down'), which is the substrate release state (r.m.s.d. for alignment = ~0.2 Å, Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Interpretation based on established knowledge of transporter mechanisms

claim: The HiSiaQM conformation is the same as the previous megabody-bound PpSiaQM structures in amphipol and a nanodisc.
source: This is the same conformation as the previous megabody-bound PpSiaQM structures in amphipol and a nanodisc (Davies et al., 2023) and also the same as the recently reported lower resolution (4.7 Å) megabody-bound HiSiaQM structure in a nanodisc (Peter et al., 2022).
evidence: Structural comparison with previously published structures

claim: 3DVA of HiSiaQM reconstructions shows only very subtle motion at the dimer interface and does not show any global elevator motions in the final reconstruction.
source: Three-dimensional variability analysis (3DVA) (Punjani and Fleet, 2021) of our HiSiaQM reconstructions shows only very subtle motion at the dimer interface and does not show any global elevator motions in the final reconstruction (Video 1).
evidence: Computational analysis of cryo-EM data shown in video

claim: The inward-open conformation is the resting state of the transporter under experimental conditions.
source: That we observe the inward-open conformation without either a bound P-subunit or fiducial marker suggests that this is the resting state of the transporter under experimental conditions (in the absence of a membrane bilayer, membrane potential, and chemical gradients).
evidence: Inference from the observation that this conformation is observed without binding partners or fiducial markers

claim: Both dimers form through an interface between the Q-subunits of the monomers.
source: Both dimers form through an interface between the Q-subunits of the monomers.
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM structures

claim: The relatively flat sides of the Q-subunits are positioned adjacent to each other in an interface that is not intimately connected by side-chain interactions.
source: The relatively flat sides of the Q-subunits are positioned adjacent to each other in an interface that is not intimately connected by side-chain interactions (Figure 2a).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM structures shown in figure

claim: The parallel dimer has slightly lower resolution at the dimer interface (scaffold region) compared to the antiparallel dimer when refined using dimeric masks.
source: When refined using dimeric masks, the parallel dimer has slightly lower resolution at the dimer interface (scaffold region) compared to the antiparallel dimer.
evidence: Observation from cryo-EM data processing and refinement

claim: Local refinement of each monomer within the parallel dimer improved the resolution at the scaffold region, suggesting this is perhaps a relatively dynamic interface.
source: Local refinement of each monomer within the parallel dimer improved the resolution at the scaffold region, suggesting this is perhaps a relatively dynamic interface.

claim: The buried interface area is small (~200 Å2) for the antiparallel configuration, and even smaller (~100 Å2) for the parallel configuration.
source: The buried interface area is small (~200 Å2) for the antiparallel configuration, and even smaller (~100 Å2) for the parallel configuration (Krissinel and Henrick, 2007).
evidence: Quantitative calculation from structural data using established methods

claim: The majority of the interface for these dimers must be mediated by lipid molecules that bridge between the monomers.
source: Further still, the parallel interface area is formed by a small number of residues at the N-termini, which have modest resolution. The majority of the interface for these dimers must therefore be mediated by lipid molecules that bridge between the monomers, some of which we observe directly in the cryo-EM maps (discussed later).
evidence: Inference from the small protein interface area and observation of lipids in the maps

claim: Small interfaces have been observed in the elevator-type Na+/H+ antiporter NhaA from E. coli.
source: Small interfaces have been observed in the elevator-type Na+/H+ antiporter NhaA from E. coli (Gupta et al., 2017) and throughout the SLC26 family (Chang et al., 2019) (also elevator-type)
evidence: Comparison with other published structures

claim: Small interfaces have been observed throughout the SLC26 family.
source: Small interfaces have been observed in the elevator-type Na+/H+ antiporter NhaA from E. coli (Gupta et al., 2017) and throughout the SLC26 family (Chang et al., 2019) (also elevator-type)
evidence: Comparison with other published structures

claim: The HiSiaQM interfaces are much smaller than other dimeric ion transporter superfamily members, such as VcINDY, MtrF, and YdaH, which have buried interface areas of ~1800–2100 Å2.
source: but the HiSiaQM interfaces are much smaller than other dimeric ion transporter superfamily members, such as the TRAP-related symporter VcINDY, a divalent anion/Na+ symporter (DASS) from Vibrio cholerae (Mulligan et al., 2016; Mancusso et al., 2012; Nie et al., 2017), and the antimicrobial efflux pumps MtrF (Su et al., 2015) and YdaH (Bolla et al., 2015), which are all elevator-type homodimers with buried interface areas of ~1800–2100 Å2.

claim: The topology of HiSiaQM is similar to the non-fused PpSiaQM, aside from the additional fusion helix that links the Q- and M-subunits across the membrane.
source: The topology of HiSiaQM is similar to the non-fused PpSiaQM, aside from the additional fusion helix that links the Q- and M-subunits across the membrane (Figure 2c).

claim: The fusion helix starts on the cytoplasmic side, packing against the Q-subunit and crossing the membrane vertically, then turns 90° and runs laterally before forming a loop and connecting to the M-subunit on the periplasmic side.
source: The helix starts on the cytoplasmic side, packing against the Q-subunit and crossing the membrane vertically, then turns 90° and runs laterally (perpendicular to the membrane) before forming a loop and connecting to the M-subunit on the periplasmic side (Figure 2a–c).
evidence: Structural observation from cryo-EM structure shown in figures

claim: HiSiaQM purified in L-MNG and DDM was characterised by sedimentation velocity analytical ultracentrifugation (SV-AUC), resulting in two distinct species in each of the samples.

claim: SV-AUC analysis suggests that HiSiaQM is present as a monomer and a dimer in both L-MNG and DDM.
